transcript.content: Hello, it's nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is… well, my life at home has started to revolve around not seeing spiders. I know that probably sounds a bit silly when I say it out loud, especially as a grown woman, but it’s become this constant arranging and rearranging of things.

For example, I keep putting off doing laundry if it means going down into the basement. I’ll let it pile up far longer than I should because I just can’t make myself go down there. And the garden shed is another one—I avoid it as much as possible, even if I need something simple from inside. I’ve actually paid people to do small jobs around the house that I’m perfectly capable of doing myself, just because it would mean going into those spaces where there might be spiders.

It’s embarrassing, really. I know how irrational it sounds, but in the moment I just can’t seem to push through it, and it’s starting to feel like my own house is being run by where I think they might be.
When you think about spiders, does the fear feel excessive or uncontrollable, and does it affect other parts of your life beyond just avoiding places like the basement or garden shed?

Yes… yes, it does feel excessive. I mean, I can say that sitting here, perfectly calmly, that a spider in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to do anything to me. I know that. I’m a teacher, I’m not someone who thinks every spider is actually dangerous in a rational sense.

But the moment I picture one—like one dropping out of a cardboard box, or sitting right near the washing machine when I’m reaching in for clothes—it’s as if it becomes this enormous, threatening thing in my mind. Not just unpleasant, but… menacing. My whole reaction feels completely out of proportion, and I’m embarrassed by that, because part of me is watching myself think it and thinking, “This is ridiculous,” but I still can’t make the fear shrink down to a normal size.
